question: How do interruptions change the force of a figure when it returns?
intro: Repeated notes, abrupt gaps and leaping figures make Scarbo difficult to keep in focus. Andriy Makarevych returns for this finale: the preceding Le Gibet uses OE1FEU’s separate recording, not the same pianist or session.

sections.label: Whispered drumming
sections.mNote: repeated notes interrupt isolated low gestures

sections.label: The dance takes shape
sections.mNote: leaping figures replace the opening hesitations

sections.label: Figures enlarged and reshuffled
sections.mNote: contrasting gestures accumulate force in successive surges

sections.label: The drumming recalled
sections.mNote: opening repeated-note texture returns in a darker register

sections.label: The dance rebuilt
sections.mNote: earlier moving figures return through changing registers

sections.label: The last large crest
sections.mNote: the piano sustains its greatest late pressure

sections.label: A vanishing close
sections.mNote: the force collapses into light final gestures

cues.title: Attack, tremble, wait
cues.text: The opening sets an isolated low gesture against very quiet repeated notes. Do not hurry to find a continuous tune: the interruptions and the sound left hanging between attacks are part of the material.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 23: Modéré, low gesture, très fondu, en trémolo and pauses. The report’s first half-minute alternates low-level attacks with sparse or zero-onset windows.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance breaks out
cues.text: The hesitant opening gives way to leaping, more continuous figures. Listen for the contrast between this moving texture and the whispered drumming; both will remain available for Ravel to interrupt and recombine.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 23–24 move from the opening through En accélérant to Vif. A measured change at 0:36 and higher relative level around 0:35–0:50 anchor the approximate region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dwarf in the room
cues.text: Bertrand’s Scarbo laughs in the shadow of an alcove, scratches the curtains and spins on one foot. The poem does not supply a literal cue sheet for every piano gesture; it supplies a creature who appears, changes size and disappears.
cues.evidence: The poem printed before Scarbo is the later Scarbo text in Bertrand’s collection, not the earlier poem of the same title: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2

cues.title: A sudden loss of weight
cues.text: After the early burst, the sound retreats sharply. The interruption makes the next accumulation matter: keep the preceding active figures in memory rather than treating the quiet stretch as a fresh beginning.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −12.9 dB at 1:35 to −31.4 at 1:45, with zero detected onsets at 1:40 and a strong boundary at 1:46. No precise rest length is claimed.

cues.title: The next surge grows
cues.text: The piano regains weight across this passage, reaching a more sustained burst than the preceding retreat. Listen for the way short gestures can accumulate pressure without becoming one long singing melody.
cues.evidence: The 2:08 boundary is followed by a rise from −21.3 dB at 2:05 to −9.5 at 2:35. The cue describes the file’s contour, not a particular chord progression.

cues.title: Three different dedications
cues.text: Ravel dedicates each movement to a different musical colleague: Ondine to Harold Bauer, Le Gibet to Jean Marnold and Scarbo to Rudolph Ganz. These dedications belong to the published score; they are not the personnel of the premiere.
cues.evidence: Dedications printed on Durand pp. 3, 17 and 23; also catalogued at https://imslp.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(Ravel%2C_Maurice).

cues.title: Follow a gesture’s outline
cues.text: Choose a short pattern and follow its rhythm and direction, not just its register. Ravel can move a figure across the keyboard, enlarge its intervals or surround it with thicker chords without making it entirely new.
cues.evidence: A movement-wide listening task grounded in the recurring repeated-note and leaping figures of Durand pp. 23–42. It does not identify a particular motivic entry at 3:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Another crest approaches
cues.text: A renewed rise carries the music towards the large surge in the next half-minute. Compare the repeated build-and-retreat pattern with Ondine: here the contrasts are more abrupt, with less continuous surface linking them.
cues.evidence: The report marks a boundary at 4:16 and rises to −7.3 dB at 4:25, with high-level windows through 4:40. The comparison concerns recorded contours, not a claim that the movements share themes.

cues.title: Do not mistake a retreat
cues.text: The piano gives up some of the recent force, then makes a short renewed attack. Listen beyond each drop in level: a retreat in Scarbo can prepare an interruption rather than a secure ending.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −8.3 dB at 4:40 to −21.7 at 4:55, rises to −9.9 at 5:00 and falls again by 5:05. The strong 5:08 boundary follows this unstable span.

cues.title: Larger than the room
cues.text: The poem’s dwarf grows until he seems as high as a Gothic cathedral. His body then becomes translucent and pale, like a candle going out. Growth and disappearance are linked in the text, rather than ending with a defeated monster.
cues.evidence: Final two paragraphs of the exact poem reproduced in the score: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2. This context is not mapped to individual notes.

cues.title: A darker recollection
cues.text: The whispered repeated-note texture has returned in a lower register. It recalls the opening’s discontinuous behaviour, but the later surroundings change its effect: memory of the large intervening surges now sits behind the quiet sound.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 34–35 explicitly reprise the introductory low gesture and repeated-note writing, moving into the bass. The 5:08 change leads to very low-level windows at 5:20–5:45 and a gradual recovery after 5:50; alignment is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Movement gathers again
cues.text: The piano rebuilds an active texture after the quiet recollection. Listen for familiar patterns in a different balance of registers: returning material need not return with its original weight or brightness.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 35–38 restore moving figures after the introductory recall. The report marks changes at 6:30 and 6:44, with increasing brightness and level around 6:35–6:45; no exact thematic downbeat is identified.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep rhythm and register separate
cues.text: Try to follow the pulse of the repeated figures while their position on the keyboard changes. What sounds newly brilliant may be an older gesture placed higher, rather than the arrival of an unrelated idea.
cues.evidence: General listening task based on the score’s redistribution of repeated-note and leaping figures. The cue makes no pitch, bar or instrumental-entry claim at 7:12.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The surge is interrupted
cues.text: A forceful burst gives way to another sharp retreat. Compare the amount of sound before and after it; Scarbo’s momentum repeatedly depends on a sudden reduction as well as on accumulation.
cues.evidence: The report reaches −9.7 dB at 7:35, then drops to −21.6 at 7:45; a measured boundary at 7:42 lies in the retreat.

cues.title: Build towards the last crest
cues.text: The final large accumulation sustains its pressure for longer than the preceding burst. Follow the rise across several phrases, not just the individual attacks: the coming withdrawal will depend on how much weight has been gathered.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −16.3 dB at 8:10 to −6.7 at 8:40, the loudest five-second window in the report. The span at 8:30–8:45 remains relatively high.

cues.title: A crest with aftershocks
cues.text: The last great rise does not descend evenly. Listen for the renewed bursts inside the overall retreat, then compare the weight of these attacks with the lighter gestures waiting at the end.
cues.evidence: After −6.7 dB at 8:40, level falls to −18.3 at 9:00 but rises again to −9.1 at 9:10. The 8:54 and 9:24 boundaries bracket the uneven closing retreat.

cues.title: Vanishing rather than triumph
cues.text: Ravel lets the closing gestures become light and brief instead of ending with the preceding weight. The final page says “without slowing”: disappearance need not mean a grand ritardando or a heavy final chord.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 42 ends with ppp repeated sonorities, small final gestures and Sans ralentir. The report falls sharply around 9:24 and remains far below the crest at 9:25–9:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Accelerate out of the interruptions
transitions.how: The isolated opening gesture and repeated-note tremble give way to rising figures marked En accélérant, then Vif. Wider keyboard leaps and more continuous attacks turn the hesitant start into moving dance material. The piano itself supplies the change of scale: no extra players arrive to create the force.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 23–24; measured boundaries at 0:36 and 0:50 with higher level than the preceding sparse windows. This is a passage estimate, not exact alignment of Vif.

transitions.title: Rebuild from the shortened gestures
transitions.how: A reduction in force interrupts the early dance. The next accumulation reuses its short figures, allowing changes of register, spacing and attack to enlarge them. The join is therefore a rebuilding after interruption rather than the continuous presentation of a second long melody.
transitions.evidence: The 1:46 retreat is followed by a strong boundary at 2:08 and the 2:05–2:35 level rise. The score supplies the short-figure writing; this section does not name an exact harmonic arrival.

transitions.title: The opening returns below the crest
transitions.how: Ravel cuts back from forceful figures to the introductory low gesture and whispered repeated notes. Their later placement reaches farther into the bass, while pauses again interrupt the flow. Recognisable material returns, but it now follows a much larger accumulation: the change of register and scale makes the recollection less like a restart.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 34–35 reprise the introduction. A strong 5:08 boundary precedes the low-level, sparse 5:10–5:45 region. The first recalled note is not independently timed.

transitions.title: Moving figures emerge from the whisper
transitions.how: The repeated-note background leads back towards moving figures and the earlier dance gestures. Register and the distribution of sustained and moving notes change as the piano gains weight. This is not a literal replay of the first dance: the quiet recall has changed its point of departure, and the fragments rebuild across several phrases.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 35–38 move from the introductory recall into transformed moving figures. Measured changes at 6:30, 6:44 and 6:58 anchor a broad rebuilding region, not a single thematic entrance.

transitions.title: Keep the accumulation under pressure
transitions.how: The later figures accumulate into a sustained high-level span. Wide-ranging piano writing and successive attacks keep the phrase under pressure across the join; there is no intervening silent reset. The crest is a large-scale result of the rebuilding, rather than a separate melody announced at the boundary.
transitions.evidence: The report rises across 8:10–8:40, with its highest window at 8:40 and high values at 8:30–8:45. No chordal analysis is inferred from those levels.

transitions.title: Cut the weight, keep the motion
transitions.how: After the last forceful bursts, the piano sheds its weight and leaves light repeated sonorities and short closing gestures. The score’s Sans ralentir keeps the end from turning into an emphatic slow conclusion. Ravel joins the huge late span to its disappearance by changing density and force, not by adding a triumphant final statement.
transitions.evidence: Durand p. 42; the 9:24 measured boundary and fall to −29.9 dB at 9:25 place the withdrawal. The final notes are not aligned individually.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
